scenes.title: The accountability problem
sentences: Restoration and carbon projects are funded on claims: hectares restored, vegetation recovered, trees surviving.
Funders and auditors can rarely check those claims themselves, or see where each number came from.
GroundTruth is a screening tool for that gap. It lines up what a project claims against what can be observed, and states plainly what it cannot show.
It is not a fraud detector, and it does not replace an audit. A gap between claim and evidence is a reason to look closer, never a verdict.
The benchmark cases on this public page are simulated, and labelled. Everything after this uses a project created live, with real satellite data.

scenes.title: The NGO: sign in and open a project
sentences: Let's follow a restoration NGO, signing in with a demonstration account.
What this user can open or change is decided by the server, not the page. The dashboard also lists a shared reference project with no observations, so we open our own.
This demonstration project is in the Sahyadri foothills near Pune, India, created by uploading a hand-drawn boundary. It is not a registered project.
The progress bar shows what is done: boundary, document, satellite data, assessment and claims. Climate data is still missing.

scenes.title: Boundary, documents and claim extraction
sentences: The boundary is stored with a checksum, and measured on an equal-area projection: about two thousand and eighteen hectares.
On the Evidence tab the NGO uploads its design document, stored with a SHA-256 checksum so it cannot be changed unnoticed.
GroundTruth then lists the statements it recognises. This is plain pattern matching, not a language model, and these are candidates only. Nothing here is verified.
It found five: a restored area, a greenness change, sapling survival, a carbon figure, and a rise in bird species richness.
I have added all five as claims. Adding a claim does not verify it, and the original wording stays beside it.

scenes.title: Real satellite observations
sentences: To get satellite evidence, the NGO requests observations for the boundary. A background worker downloads Sentinel-2 images from Microsoft Planetary Computer, masks cloud, and reduces each year to one value.
This request covered 2021 to 2026, January to March, at most twenty percent cloud. It finished, with project-area coverage above ninety-five percent every year.

The satellite's reflectance measurements are observations. The indices computed from them, such as NDVI, are derived indicators, and each row is badged that way. A model estimate would carry a diamond. There are none here.
The table lists the exact scene identifiers behind each year, so anyone can repeat the calculation.
NDVI shows how green the land looks from space. It is not carbon, tree survival or biodiversity, and these values are not validated against field data.
The series is not a clean rise: greenness peaks in 2023, then falls back. The assessment reads this as no clear change.

scenes.title: Claim assessment
sentences: On the verification tab, each claim is judged on its own evidence.
The area claim is only partly consistent. The claimed nineteen hundred hectares fits inside the boundary, but a boundary shows where a project works, not how much land was restored.
The greenness claim, up 0.05, is consistent with the observed change of about 0.051. That describes greenness. It does not show the project caused it.

Three claims are marked not enough evidence to test: survival needs field surveys, carbon needs biomass measurement or a registry record, and bird species need wildlife surveys. Unverified does not mean false. It means the evidence has not been supplied.
Attribution is inconclusive: there are no observations from before treatment, no comparison areas and no climate series. So GroundTruth makes no causal claim.

scenes.title: Evidence dossier and audit ledger
sentences: Everything the platform knows can be exported as a technical dossier for an auditor.
The ZIP holds the assessment, claims, observations with scene identifiers, documents and provenance, with a checksum manifest.
Each download is sealed in an audit ledger. Records are chained to one another, and the page recomputes the chain every time it loads.
The new report-sealed record appears here. The ledger is not externally timestamped or signed, so it detects alteration, deletion and reordering, but cannot prove when a record was written.
In testing, altering one stored record in the database made the page report a failed integrity check. Restoring it returned the status to verified.

scenes.title: Funder, auditor and what comes next
sentences: The funder has view access. They can read claims, observations and the ledger, but see no upload or request controls, and the server refuses those actions even when attempted directly.
The auditor can download the dossier, and check any file they were given against the ledger record that sealed it.
Here, the file is confirmed byte-for-byte identical to the sealed report.
This is an early screening tool. Next: observations from before a project began, climate and comparison-area data so attribution becomes possible, and field validation of the satellite values.
GroundTruth. What was claimed, what was observed, and what cannot yet be shown.
